title: ISO/IEC 17025 — Testing and Calibration Laboratories
shortDescription: The standard for general testing/calibration labs — and the precise comparison to ISO 15189 that exams love to ask for.
genZNote: Your lab result needs evidence, traceability and competence, not 'trust me bro.'

sections.heading: What It Is and Who It's For
bullets: Full title: 'General requirements for the competence of testing and calibration laboratories.'

Applies broadly to TESTING laboratories (chemical, materials, environmental, food, microbiology outside a clinical context, etc.) and CALIBRATION laboratories — deliberately NOT limited to any one industry, unlike ISO 15189's medical-specific focus.
Jointly published by ISO and IEC (hence 'ISO/IEC 17025'), first issued 1999, current edition ISO/IEC 17025:2017.

sections.heading: Core Requirements
bullets: Impartiality — the laboratory's activities must be carried out impartially, structurally and behaviourally protected from commercial, financial, or other pressures that could compromise judgement.
Competence — personnel must be demonstrably competent for the specific tests/calibrations they perform.
Validity of results — methods must be validated as fit for purpose, and measurement uncertainty must be evaluated and reported where relevant.
Measurement traceability — calibration results must be traceable to the International System of Units (SI) through an unbroken chain of calibrations.
Impartiality and confidentiality together with technical competence are what distinguish an accredited testing/calibration lab from one that simply claims to follow good practice.

sections.heading: Two Categories of Requirements
bullets: Management requirements — organizational structure, document control, corrective/preventive action, internal audit, management review — broadly similar in spirit to ISO 9001's management-system elements.

Technical requirements — personnel competence, facilities/environmental conditions, equipment, measurement traceability, sampling, and handling of test/calibration items — the technical substance specific to lab work.

sections.heading: Why These Are Not Interchangeable
sections.body: A materials-testing laboratory would seek ISO/IEC 17025 accreditation, not ISO 15189, because its work has nothing to do with patient specimens or clinical interpretation. Conversely, a hospital pathology lab uses ISO 15189 specifically because it needs the patient-safety and clinical-phase requirements that a general testing standard doesn't cover. A lab that does BOTH clinical testing and general calibration work could, in principle, be accredited against both standards for their respective scopes — they are not mutually exclusive, just scoped differently.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: ISO/IEC 17025 sets general competence requirements for testing and calibration laboratories of any kind, distinguished from ISO 15189's medical-laboratory-specific scope by its broader applicability and its management+technical requirement structure.
keyFacts: Jointly published by ISO and IEC; current edition ISO/IEC 17025:2017; first issued 1999.
Applies to any testing/calibration lab, not limited to medical/clinical contexts.
Core pillars: impartiality, competence, validity of results, measurement traceability to SI units.
Structured around Management requirements + Technical requirements, unlike ISO 15189's three-phase (pre/examination/post) structure.
In India, NABL accredits labs against both ISO/IEC 17025 (testing/calibration) and ISO 15189 (medical) — under separate accreditation programmes.
commonConfusion: ISO/IEC 17025 and ISO 15189 are sibling standards but scoped differently — a materials-testing lab needs 17025, a clinical pathology lab needs 15189.
Traceability under 17025 is specifically to the SI unit system — not just 'traceable to some reference', but to internationally recognised measurement units.

highYieldFacts: ISO/IEC 17025 applies broadly to testing/calibration labs; ISO 15189 applies specifically to medical laboratories.
ISO/IEC 17025 is jointly published by ISO and IEC; current edition 2017.
Both standards are, in India, accredited through NABL — but under separate, distinct accreditation programmes.
commonTraps: Do not say ISO/IEC 17025 is 'the medical lab standard' — that is ISO 15189's job specifically.
Do not conflate 'measurement uncertainty' (a quantified doubt range around a result) with 'measurement error' (an actual deviation) — 17025 requires evaluating/reporting the former.
mustRemember: 17025's two requirement categories: Management requirements and Technical requirements.
Impartiality is a structural/behavioural requirement under 17025, protecting against commercial or financial pressure on results.

confusedTerms.distinction: ISO 15189 is scoped specifically to medical/clinical laboratories and structured around the pre-examination/examination/post-examination phases; ISO/IEC 17025 applies to any testing or calibration laboratory and is structured around management + technical requirements.

possibleQuestions: Which ISO/IEC standard applies to a general materials-testing laboratory — 15189 or 17025?
